description: Routing in the App Router is file-system based, using folders to define paths and special files (like page.tsx, layout.tsx, template.tsx, route.ts) to define UI. Routes run inside a Server Component context by default, preserving layouts and minimizing component re-renders when navigating between nested dynamic paths.

constraints.title: Use Only Valid App Router Files Inside Route Segments
constraints.problem: Placing utility files, test files, or components directly in dynamic routing directories can confuse the bundler or cause route resolution errors if named incorrectly.
constraints.whyItMatters: Next.js enforces strict routing rules. Any folder containing a `route.ts` or `page.tsx` defines an addressable route. Exposing other files in these folders can accidentally expose internal routes if they match the framework pattern, or lead to deployment bundling inflation.
forbiddenPatterns: Placing internal components directly inside route folders without prefixing them with an underscore or keeping them in separate components folder
Co-locating route.ts and page.tsx inside the exact same routing folder segment
allowedPatterns: Storing non-routing components inside a localized components/ directory outside the app/ directory
Using private folders prefixed with an underscore (_components) inside route directories to bypass routing
productionRisks: Conflicting route resolutions resulting in 404 or 500 errors
Exposure of internal utility functions as public API endpoints
Increased bundler payload from unorganized routing files
architectureImplications: Requires isolating domain components from folder routing structures
optimizationGuidance: Use private folder naming conventions (_folder) to organize tests or mocks within the route structure safely
quickFixes: Move nested component files to an external components/ folder, or rename the local folder prefix to an underscore (_components)
architectureSuggestions: Keep the app/ folder lightweight, holding only routing folders and route-specific layouts/pages, while keeping structural components elsewhere

invalid: // Inside app/dashboard/layout.tsx and app/dashboard/route.ts in the same folder segment
valid: // Inside app/dashboard/page.tsx, with API actions separated to app/api/dashboard/route.ts

constraints.title: Prevent Co-location of Route Handlers and Pages in Same Segment
constraints.problem: Creating a route.ts (or route.js) and a page.tsx (or page.js) inside the exact same directory will crash the compiler or cause route mismatches during execution.
constraints.whyItMatters: Next.js App Router treats route.ts files as raw HTTP dynamic endpoints (handling GET, POST, DELETE, etc.) and page.tsx files as component rendering targets. If both exist in the same route folder, Next.js cannot determine whether to render HTML or serve JSON. It will throw a compilation error or ignore one of them entirely.
forbiddenPatterns: Creating app/api/items/page.tsx and app/api/items/route.ts together inside the items/ directory
allowedPatterns: Moving route handlers into a separate app/api/ directory mapping
Keeping only page.tsx inside the user-facing app/ route folders
productionRisks: Server routing crashing during dynamic API requests
Total loss of page or API route access in production environments
architectureImplications: Forces separating front-end rendering routing from back-end API route controllers
Enforces architectural purity in directory layout mappings
optimizationGuidance: Isolate all JSON/HTTP API endpoints to a dedicated app/api/ subfolder to keep routes clear and robust
quickFixes: Move the route.ts file out of the page.tsx folder, typically into a dedicated app/api/... segment
architectureSuggestions: Use Server Actions inside pages/components for mutations instead of route handlers, completely eliminating the need for co-located route.ts API endpoints

invalid: // app/products/page.tsx and app/products/route.ts inside the same folder
valid: // app/products/page.tsx for user UI, app/api/products/route.ts for raw data REST operations

constraints.title: Always Define default.tsx in Parallel Routes to Prevent 404 Navigation Failures
constraints.problem: Omitting a default.tsx (or default.jsx) fallback file inside Parallel Route slots (@slot) will cause 404 errors during clientside page reload or navigation.
constraints.whyItMatters: During client-side navigation, Next.js keeps track of currently rendered parallel slots. However, on a full browser page refresh (reload), Next.js cannot retrieve the previous slot state. If it cannot find a corresponding `default.tsx` file for that parallel route slot at the current sub-URL, it immediately crashes and serves a 404. Defining a default fallback layout is mandatory to ensure navigation robustness.
forbiddenPatterns: Defining parallel slots (e.g. @analytics) under layout folders without providing a sibling default.tsx file
allowedPatterns: Creating a default.tsx inside every parallel slot directory returning a fallback layout or null: export default function Default() { return null; }
productionRisks: Users experiencing unexpected 404 page crashes on reload
Incomplete routing state transitions during deep link share clicks
Critical dashboard layouts failing to load under specific client-side navigations
architectureImplications: Mandates structuring parallel slots as self-contained state fallbacks
Enforces robust fallback definition boundaries across dynamic layout folders
optimizationGuidance: Ensure default.tsx returns a matching shell component or null to safely bridge hydration transitions during full page reloads
quickFixes: Create a default.tsx file in your parallel slot directory that returns null or a matching structural loader component
architectureSuggestions: Build parallel route slots with complete layout boundaries (holding layout, page, and default files) to ensure seamless independent rendering capability
